utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody, and you, in particular, Mr. Registrar. Can I ask you to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Please take a seat. Mr. Wubben, appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution, together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And also good morning to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends and colleagues. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries before we start with the new witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one, which is that, as I mentioned to my learned friend, with this witness, who may be controversial, may give his opinions on a number of subjects, we would appreciate if my learned friend would not lead at all once we get to his arrival in Srebrenica. I believe it's a matter we have a right to insist on, and we would insist in this instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, of course. The practice is, and I made it clear from the very word go, that we would -- although, strictly speaking, leading questions are not procedurally correct, we allow them here, provided there is no objection. The moment there is an objection, I mean, we stick to the Rules --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because I don't want to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But do --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What I mean is, because I don't want to be jumping up the whole time, I made that clear to my friend this morning. Obviously, the background matters, where he was born he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not referring to that. Mr. Wubben, who is leading this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm also -- we've discussed this a little bit this morning, Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and myself. We would like you to stick to the basics -- to the point and try to restrict your questions to what is basically relevant to this case. On the other hand, we also want to make it clear that we will not be imposing any deadlines as regards this witness. In other words, you will have all the time you require, both of you, both Defence and Prosecution, of course. On the other hand, that doesn't mean that you can go on and on ad infinitum, okay? Good. Could you bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we proceed any further, I want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Welcome to this Tribunal. I am the Presiding Judge. My name is Carmel Agius, and I come from the island of Malta. At my right is Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt from Denmark; to my left, Judge Albin Eser from Germany. We are presiding over this case against Naser Oric. You are about to give evidence, and according to our Rules, before you do so, you are bound to make a solemn declaration, a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath, and tantamount to an oath, such that you will be testifying the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is going to be handed now by Madam Usher. Please read it out to -- read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. The procedure here is a very simple one, more or less, the same as it is in domestic jurisdictions. You have been summoned here as a witness by the Prosecution, and accordingly, Mr. Wubben, who is lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case, will ask you a series of questions. He will then be followed by Mr. Jones, who is co-counsel in the Defence team for Naser Oric. Your testimony is expected to last a few days, so I have to tell you that if, at any time, you feel tired and you need a break, please do let me know and I'll discuss with my two colleagues and decide what to do. However, your responsibility, your foremost responsibility is to answer all questions, irrespective of who is putting these questions, in other words, whether the Prosecution or the Defence. Your responsibility is to answer those questions, all of them, independently of where they come from, truthfully and fully and to the best of your ability. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In the meanwhile, you might have noticed that co-counsel Ms. Joanne Richardson joined the Prosecution team, and further, as an issue, there are maps upon your general request to hand them over prior to the start. There are two maps available for you. The maps are kind of divided into the maps from Tuzla to Srebrenica, so that means west to east, and Zvornik to Zepa, which means north to south. I tender these on your behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Mujkanovic. I will start my questions now. Please confirm for the Judges your name -- your full name is Nedret Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And you were born on the 30th of May, 1961, in Brcko, Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your ethnic origin is Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your current occupation is plastic surgeon in the University Medical Centre, Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your former occupation is resident pathologist?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: You have participated in politics as a member of the local Tuzla parliament from 1990 until 1997?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Regarding military service, in 1980 and 1981, you served one year compulsory military service with the JNA in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your educational background is that, after the army, you attended medical training at the university for six years?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And after those medical studies, you were a general practitioner?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And after that, you specialised in pathology?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And you conducted autopsies in the hospital in Tuzla in the field of training of students?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this latter phase in his career, I think he better identify it within a time frame. When did he become a pathologist, a qualified pathologist, and when did he start conducting these autopsies? Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1988, I worked as an assistant at the medical school in the pathology department. I trained students in pathology and pathological anatomy. Part of their training was also to conduct autopsies. One of the drills used for training medical students included autopsy, and I stayed in that capacity until March 1992. I worked as an assistant. From March 1992 on, I worked as a surgeon. I have been a surgeon to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, now. Thank you, witness, and thank you, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'll proceed, Dr. Mujkanovic. Is it correct that in May 1992, in the Tuzla area, a war field hospital needed to be set up?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did you volunteer to go?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did you also set up war field hospitals in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's actually the same hospital. It was in Kalesija municipality, about 20 kilometres to the east of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And there came a time in July 1992 that you met with Professor Dr. Radevic, and that he clarified to you that he had been tasked by the War Presidency of Tuzla to resolve the problem of having to send a surgeon to Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And were you considered as a candidate for that job?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And was your response to this request positive?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Why were you willing to volunteer for such a mission?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, there was a difficult situation related to accommodating the wounded and injured persons. At that point Srebrenica was an isolated enclave, as it remained throughout the war. There was no possibility of transporting the wounded and injured on to Tuzla Hospital. As a result of that, people died and succumbed to their injuries. A war field hospital needed to be set up following the war surgical doctrines in order to be able to deal with the problem of the wounded and injured people as soon as possible in the Srebrenica area and the mid-Podrinje area. I volunteered, or rather, I accepted an offer from Dr. Bozina Radevic, who was my boss. He was head of surgery at the University Medical Centre in Tuzla. And in July, I started my preparations to leave for Srebrenica, or rather, to be infiltrated into the Srebrenica area, which at the time, as I said, was entirely surrounded and isolated. It was impossible --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Mujkanovic, here I have to stop you because I have another question. What was your projected function and tasking regarding that war field hospital -- that war hospital? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Primarily, to establish a war hospital based on the principles of the war surgical doctrine. That means to establish a hospital to function at war, not in peace. Then to establish a well-functioning reception of the wounded, the moment they are wounded, where they're wounded, their transportation to the hospital, according to the rules of the modern medicine. The hospital had to be equipped with all the surgical instruments and the necessary implements, and more surgeons had to be enabled to arrive in the territory of Srebrenica in order to provide for the needs of some 80 to 100.000 people who were present in the area at the time, from Kamenica to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question: Was the war hospital in Srebrenica planned to function within the organisation of the Srebrenica armed forces?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not discussed at that time how it was supposed to function, but since early on, I worked as a war surgeon at the Kalesija war hospital. There was a rule for the war hospitals to provide care both for the wounded members of the army - at the time it was Territorial Defence; later on to become the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina - as well as civilians who would be wounded during an attack of shelling or an air raid and requiring surgical intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you, after preparation, actually leave for Srebrenica on the 22nd of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of July, 1992, an action commenced with the aim of infiltrating a medical team with people who were carrying the entire medical equipment necessary for the setting up of the war hospital, in the direction of Srebrenica. However, this did not happen on the 22nd of July, or on the subsequent days, because it was impossible for the entire team to be infiltrated through the enemy lines in the area north of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did Zeljko Knez, the then regional TO commander in Tuzla, assign Major Nurif Rizvanovic and his 16th Muslim Brigade in his mission in order to escort you and your group?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: After an initial attempt to reach the area of Crni Vrh, in which we were prevented in the locality of Bajkovica, because we were prevented by the enemy forces, the following day I returned to the Kalesija war hospital where I asked for a different sort of an attempt to be organised for us to be infiltrated with the equipment necessary for establishing a war hospital. We were carrying the equipment on our backs. Mr. Muharem Efendic, the commander of the 4th Tactical Group, contacted the commander of the Territorial Defence in Tuzla, whereupon Mr. Knez, the commander of the district staff of the Tuzla Territorial Defence, assigned Nurif Rizvanovic and his group to accompany us, escort us, to the free territory of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Mujkanovic, is it correct that your fourth attempt to cross enemy lines was successful, and that this crossing happened on the 29th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. After having tried, together with Nurif Rizvanovic, to cross the enemy lines, it was only on our fourth successful attempt to cross the enemy lines, get into the area of Crni Vrh, which was behind the enemy lines and was occupied by the Serb forces at that point in time, we then headed in the direction of Snagovo, which was the first -- the nearest liberated area under the control of the then Territorial Defence, later to become the army of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to stop you. The 29th. Is it correct that finally, on the 5th of August, 1992, you left for your last part -- for the last part of your trip towards Srebrenica after you reached Bosnian-held territory?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In the afternoon hours of the 5th of August, heading out from the direction of Konjevic Polje, I managed to reach Gornji Potocari, the village of Susnjari, together with my team, which was in the area -- in the free area of Srebrenica. I have to say that, having arrived at Konjevic Polje on the 4th of August, the entire unit commanded by Nurif Rizvanovic in Konjevic Polje, whereas I reached Srebrenica in the company of the people who headed out with me from the start, as well as with those who were assigned to be our escorts and take us to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Whether did you arrive at Srebrenica? What date?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what appeared to be how long you would stay there in Srebrenica? For how many months in total?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: After having made the journey, which was a very unsafe one, a very risky one - our lives were continually in danger - I knew that I was going to stay there until --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Sorry, doctor. Yes, my question was, for a good understanding, for how long will you stay in Srebrenica, or were you already towards the answer. If so, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean how long I remained in Srebrenica. I stayed there until the 22nd of July, 19 -- or, rather, until the 22nd of April, 1993, after the demilitarisation of the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. That was, indeed, my question. On your arrival, who did welcome you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I entered the area of Srebrenica in the afternoon hours, at about 400 p.m., and I was welcomed by members of the Srebrenica Territorial Defence, who were holding the positions there, and several villagers also welcomed me. I waited there for about an hour and a half until Naser arrived with several other members of the Territorial Defence to take me personally to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Naser who? I suppose there are many Nasers in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Was this the first time you met Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Who did accompany Naser Oric during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: At that point I didn't know anybody there. There were some 10 to 15 people there, men, who arrived with Naser, and they arrived on a truck. It was then that I met Naser Oric for the first time, as well as Zulfo Tursunovic. There were some other people among them who I got to know later on and who I was frequently in touch with and socialised with. Some of them were my patients, because they were eventually wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, what was the function, if so, of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, this is the sort of question which I was asking my learned friend to avoid. I mean, firstly, there's no -- to put a question like that without any foundation, we've got the story so far that Mr. -- or Dr. Mujkanovic has arrived in Srebrenica and he's been asked all of a sudden to cast about and guess at what Naser Oric's function was. If he asks -- it's not the sort of question which I think is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's perfectly legitimate. The witness has just told us that, all of a sudden, in this particular circumstance, Naser Oric appeared with a number of men, and he is being asked whether he knows what function Naser Oric was filling or having on that occasion. It's a perfectly legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If my learned friend would stick to questions of what was said by the people there, what was your impression. I mean, there's no indication from the evidence that's been given that this witness will know anything about what the function is of Naser Oric at that time. He's just arrived on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely what legitimises the question, this is precisely why the question is perfectly legitimate. Go ahead. You were asked by Mr. Wubben to tell us whether you knew of any function that Naser Oric was filling or fulfilling on that occasion, if you are aware. I don't want you to speculate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't speculate. I had heard of Naser Oric only as I was passing on my way to Srebrenica. I didn't know who the commander in Srebrenica was. It was towards the latter part of my journey, as I was heading towards Srebrenica, that I was told that the commander in Srebrenica was Naser Oric. The rest I got to know when I met him, whereas I had heard previously from people who were around me that Naser Oric had been commander of the defence in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you also find out, Dr. Mujkanovic, what function Zulfo Tursunovic had, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: At that point I didn't know who Zulfo Tursunovic was or what his role was, or of any of the men who met me there, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will get back to that later on. I have the following question: What happened after that first, initial, meeting with Naser Oric and Zulfo Tursunovic? Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: We were trucked from the village of Susnjari to the town of Srebrenica itself. We stopped outside the post office building in Srebrenica. The hospital was across from the post office building. And it was in the post office building that I had a meeting, or rather, that I had opportunity to get to know some other people who were there, including two medical doctors, two colleagues of mine who had been working in the Srebrenica hospital already. This took maybe half an hour at most, and then I went to the Srebrenica Hospital, together with two doctors, colleagues of mine. We started unpacking the large sacks containing surgical instruments for the purposes of the hospital, and we practically started setting up the surgical theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, what was the function of your colleagues that you met?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: At that point nobody held any functions. They were simply doctors working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can you mention the two most important colleagues that were cooperating together with you?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: They weren't the two most important ones working with me. There was a total of seven doctors working in Srebrenica. One of them was Dr. Avdo Hasanovic, who held the function of the general manager of the hospital in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, permission to lead on the name of another colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear the question, and if it's the case of stopping you, I don't know what question you're going to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let's hear the question first, and then we'll be in a position to tell you whether it's acceptable to go ahead with it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's the question of the function of Dr. Ilijan Pilav.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, are you in a position to enlighten us on what role Dr. Ilijan Pilav filled at the time? What was his function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The doctor's name is Ilijas Pilav.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. And what was his function?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: He had no function at the time or later on. He was one of the doctors working in the hospital. I don't know of any function that he discharged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Avdo Hasanovic, apart from being a general manager of the hospital, did he also have other tasking?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the general manager of the hospital, and I believe he was a member of the War Presidency, though I'm not sure. I do know that he had the task of acting as a liaison between the hospital and the War Presidency in logistical matters. For the purposes of the hospital, in other words, food, firewood or fuel, and medicines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And who did the autopsies in the hospital, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No autopsies were performed in the hospital. There was just one autopsy performed in the hospital by myself, because the actual cause of a violent death had to be established, and this was the case with one member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, I might come back to that issue later on. From the start of your job at the hospital, what was your official function? And if you have any title, please inform the Judges.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question in terms of the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: As Dr. Avdo Hasanovic was the general manager, what was your function at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, my role was that of a war surgeon who was supposed to operate on those wounded and injured, to organise the work of the entire surgical ward, of the surgical theatre, of the reception ward, triage ward. And in actual fact, the entire time I spent in Srebrenica, and especially the first two months, was spent actually in the surgical theatre and in linking up with those surgical points that were out in the field from where those injured and wounded would then be transported to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, you confirmed to the Judges that, at that point in time, meaning August or September 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And after those months, was there any change, any change in the label of your position or your function?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in the second half of September, the operational staff of the armed forces of Srebrenica was established, and my role within the staff was that of a chief of the medical corps of the armed forces of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did -- can you tell the Court whether or not your function as a war surgeon or as a chief of the -- chief medical commander of the armed forces in Srebrenica fell within the military organisation of those armed forces?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Do you recall the number of treatments of Bosnian soldiers during a year's time at that hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: The war hospital in Srebrenica had, in one year, from 17 April 1992 to the 17th April 1993, provided for over 3.600 wounded and injured persons, out of which 1.600 were members of the army who were wounded and over 1.000 wounded civilians, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were there any statistics available of how many soldiers in the Srebrenica armed forces had been killed in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: We had approximate data in the hospital pointing to some 840 to 850 members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who had been killed. Now, I'm only mentioning members of the army here, but there were over 2.000 civilians who were killed at the time as a result of shelling or air raids directed against the town, or as a result of suffering injuries from activating land-mines and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And again, Dr. Mujkanovic, the same period of time, 17th of April, 1992 until 17th of April, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: From the 17th of April, 1992 until the 17th of April, 1993, so I'm talking about this one year of the official war in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, until the 18th of April, because it was after the 18th of April that demilitarisation took place, so that's the one year that I spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you treat yourself, in the war hospital, patients who were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serb prisoners, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: All those who were wounded or injured and were taken to the hospital in Srebrenica were treated according to ethical principles and principles of medical deontology, regardless of their religious, racial -- their religion, race, or gender, so that even those who were Serbs and were wounded were treated according to the same rules of medical practice, as had been applied to members of Bosniak or other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And did that include Serb detainees?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about detainees. I'm talking about the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What I mean, Dr. Mujkanovic, a wounded Serb patient who is as well detained in your hospital? Can you confirm that sometimes some of your patients were, as well, detainees?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that my patients were persons who were wounded, and as such were brought into the hospital and treated there. Following treatment, they were handed back to the military police. But neither I, nor any of my colleagues at the hospital, treated anyone in the status of detainees. I am not sure about the definition of detainee, I'm not sure what you mean exactly when you say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did it happen some time that there were guards before the doors of a room where a patient was curing?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to clarify. All the wounded would be brought in in shifts. They were brought in in lorries. We did not have ambulances, we used lorries to bring the patients in. We would then conduct triage. Depending on the sort of wounds that they had suffered, we would conduct surgery and treat these patients. We paid no heed as to whether these people were Bosniaks or Serbs. It would sometimes happen that, as a result of the limited space that we had at our disposal, all these people were wounded so they had to lie in the same room, altogether. Two or three days later, we would separate the Serbs, or rather, members of the Serbian army, and take them to special rooms at the hospital with special security. Guards were placed in front of these rooms, and they were in charge of the security of these Serb patients. I can say that no attack or incident ever took place at the hospital. No one ever tried to hurt those people in any way. They shared the fate of all of us who were in Srebrenica at the time, patients and civilians alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Those guards who stood guard for the doors -- in front of the doors, were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: To speak about uniforms in Srebrenica is a futile exercise. Those people were soldiers carrying weapons in order to be able to provide good security for the patients. As for uniforms, no one in Srebrenica really wore a uniform at the time. They were all wearing civilian clothes, but they were soldiers all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And they were armed?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course they were. The hospital --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And was that, in your opinion, the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness was providing an answer about the hospital. I think he should be allowed to finish that answer, because it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct, Mr. Jones. Let's go back to line 12. The question, witness, was: "Those guards who stood guard for the doors -- in front of the doors, were they in uniform?" And you were saying: "To speak about uniforms in Srebrenica is a futile exercise Those people were soldiers carrying weapons in order to be able to provide good security for the patients. As for uniforms, no one in Srebrenica really wore a uniform at the time. They were all wearing civilian clothes, but they were soldiers all the same." And then you were asked: "And they were armed?" "Of course they were. The hospital --" and you were going to explain something when you were interrupted by Mr. Wubben who asked you: "And was that, in your opinion, the military police?" So before you tell us whether it was the military police or not, could you please give us a full answer to the question, whether those people in Srebrenica were armed or not. You have already said, of course, they were, and then you said: "The hospital ..." And you were going to tell us something about the hospital. Thank you, Mr. Jones, for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a guard standing outside the hospital providing security. There was always a guard, and they took shifts. Their task was to protect the hospital from unwanted arrivals, and thus to protect the lives of nurses, doctors, and patients, as well as to foil any acts of sabotage by Serbs. Acts of sabotage often occurred in the free territory of Srebrenica, incursions by Serb sabotage units, killing people and destroying property in the Srebrenica area. This was one of their tasks, namely, to make the hospital a safe place for patients to recover and to make sure that doctors and nurses had good conditions for their work. When I spoke about Srebrenica, those people were the Territorial Defence, and no one had any uniforms. Maybe at a later stage, some people were given camouflage uniforms that were obtained in whatever way and supplied to the people in Srebrenica. Most of the soldiers, however, had no uniform or weapons. Sometimes two or three persons had to share a single rifle. Nevertheless, there had to be security for the hospital, and whoever was providing security at any given point in time had to carry a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these guards --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: These guards, these armed guards, did they form part of the armed forces as being the military police, if so, or do you -- don't you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I've never really wanted to know if those people were military police or not. They were guards; that's all I needed to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I come now to another issue, the issue of the situation in Srebrenica in that period of time, August 1992, and later on. What observations can you give to the Court of the situation in Srebrenica when it comes to the local population and any refugees?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, the conditions in that area were horrific. If there ever was hell on earth, it must have been Srebrenica in 1992 and 1993. And as you know, 1993, 1994, and 1995 were, in actual fact, something that brings shame to our civilisation. It was a time of famine, 1992 and 1993, a time of daily attacks against Srebrenica, a time of daily shellings, a time of daily air attacks, a time of poverty, a time when refugees were flooding in from the general Podrinje area; Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, Zvornik, Bratunac. Some of the areas around Srebrenica were occupied. It was a time that brings shame to late 20th century civilisation. There was no medicine to treat people with, no anaesthetics to be administered prior to surgery. It was a time when people with no weapons were faced with a situation where they had to defend themselves. They had no support and no supplies and nothing to give them a decent chance of surviving in the area. Time seemed very long. A single day in Srebrenica in that period seemed like an eternity. And some people spent as long as three years, stayed throughout from 1992 to 1995, which was when Srebrenica eventually fell. This is a time that I do not wish to revisit, as a human being or as someone who was personally involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I do understand, of course, sometimes when witnesses choose to give a more extensive answer than what they are being asked. On the other hand, I must make it clear that if we continue like this, this witness is going to be here for two weeks, easily. We have barely started the part of his evidence which is really relevant for the case that we have before us, I mean, and I invite you to go to the head, straight away, as soon as you can, and the witness to please restrict your answers. I mean, I usually give the following advice to witnesses, Mr. Mujkanovic: Namely, that the secret of giving testimony is to answer the whole question -- answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Otherwise, I'm afraid you're going to be here for a long time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be so bold, the witness was asked a very general question about his observations about the conditions of life in Srebrenica. I think he gave a very full, poignant and important answer, and we would certainly submit that the conditions, appalling conditions in Srebrenica is highly relevant to this case, and so I would beg to differ that the answer was in any way irrelevant. I would submit that it is highly irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not referring to this answer, in particular, I'm referring to all the answers that he has been giving. They are lengthy and sometimes they give more information than what is being sought, and we can't go on like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The question was very general, was very open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was not general and very open. The question was focused on August, and to clarify my own position in this respect, I'm very respectful towards an opinion when it comes to a tragedy as responded by the witness, and that's why I didn't interrupt. I interrupted him -- I waited for an interruption at that specific part that I thought it might be ended. My question was very specific. The question was: What was your observation upon your arrival in August 1992 regarding the refugees? Earlier I tried to interrupt the witness and I was prevented from it. That also took us a lot of time. For this particular delicate, may I say, opinion-sharing by the witness, I had to respect -- to give him enough to express his feelings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My question, again, if you allow me, Your Honour, my question again, Dr. Mujkanovic, and please keep it brief, what was your observation of the situation in Srebrenica regarding the refugees? What could you see in the streets of Srebrenica in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see many people in the streets, many refugees. But you must know that my job was not to watch refugees. Sometimes I would spend as many as 36 or 40 hours on end in the surgical theatre, without ever leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did that also, that situation, affect everyday lives in the street, people being distributed with food, already in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see that there may be a problem with interpretation. Dr. Mujkanovic, are you receiving interpretation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, but there was a very brief interruption towards the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's a good thing that I keep my eyes open and travelling from east to west, or from left to right. The question was the following, by Mr. Wubben: "Did that also, that situation, affect everyday lives in the street, people being distributed with food, already in August 1992?" This was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question. Are you expecting me to provide a brief answer to a question I don't understand? That's impossible. What do people out in the street have to do with food distribution? And I'm not sure what the link is imagined to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not try to do that for Mr. Wubben. Mr. Wubben, it's your question. Could you rephrase it in a way that is more understandable for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did the refugees referred to at that time, in August 1992, live in the streets, or did they live somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's a different question, isn't it? At that time everyone had a roof over their heads. Now, whether there were perhaps 15 or 20 people living packed in a single house, that's another matter. But everyone had some sort of accommodation, and there was no difference between the local population and people who had come in from outside. They all had the same treatment and enjoyed the same conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did there come a time that that situation changed? I mean that refugees started to live on the streets, or at least outside houses?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's true. That was after Konjevic Polje and Cerska had fallen. I'm talking about early March 1993. So from that time on until the demilitarisation, tens of thousands of refugees from Konjevic Polje were on their way to Srebrenica. Srebrenica could not put everyone up, so people lived outside in the streets and in public buildings, wherever they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please bear me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: When it comes to the hospital, you confirmed to the Judges, Dr. Mujkanovic, that this was a war hospital, and my next question is: Did Naser Oric ever visit the hospital to see the patients, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very often, he used to come very often, and he would see the patients. Whenever he came, he would first come to see me or the other doctors, and then he would be accompanied during his tour of the hospital. He would see patients and inquire about their help.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What do you mean by "very often"? Every now and then, on a regular basis, or every day?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Not every day, but not a week went by without him coming to visit the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And why did he visit the patients?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: He wanted to know about their health. There were many people there who were wounded; most of the people there were, in fact. He wanted to see what would happen to those people. Lots of limbs were being amputated at the time. He wanted to know about those people, whether their lives were in danger, whether they would make it. I think it was a humane instinct that drove him to come and ask questions about the fate of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did he also have to visit -- no, sorry, I will rephrase my question. Did he also visit the Serb detainees who were patients in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness said clearly that he didn't know what detainees meant. There were Serbs, some of whom who might have been in a private ward. There's another way of approaching the question without putting "detainee" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you have to go back a few questions before you can actually put this question, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay. I will rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the objection can only be sustained. Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just for a matter of clarification of the language, I remember that in earlier trials, the question has been phrased in terms of prisoners. Now you speak of detainees. I don't know whether that is a distinction in the Bosnian-Serbian language, so perhaps you could clarify whether you mean the same with detainees and prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In my opinion, "detainee" is, in general, a person who is under a form of secured guard, and a prisoner is a detainee who is imprisoned and, as such, a special function of a building, is spending his time in that building. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This even makes it more clear that you have to go a few questions back before you can put the -- just ask the witness -- you've got four more minutes to go before we break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did Naser Oric also pay special attention to Serb patients?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: He paid the same sort of attention to everyone, Bosniaks and Serbs alike. He wanted to know about everyone's health.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Including Serb patients who were guarded?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And was there any information exchanged between the hospital and the armed forces in Srebrenica at that time regarding those Serb patients?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no official exchange of information. There were some conversations, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And who did communicate that with the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Each of us. I may have, Dr. Avdo, Dr. Ilijas, Dr. Avdic. Each and any of the doctors could have been in a situation to orally report on the health of a given patient. We did not write any official reports. We would transmit information orally. Someone, for example, may have been asking about a certain patient and then we would tell them, we would tell them about the patient's health and our assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And had there also been medical reports drafted on behalf of such patients?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am now up to a new issue, and I would prefer to request for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Wubben. We will have a short break of 25 minutes, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, I will ask you some questions about this time, the first months of your arrival, August 1992, beginning September, and my question relates to the armed forces, the TO, in Srebrenica. Can you describe for the Judges the chain of command of the Territorial Defence in Srebrenica at the times -- at the months of your arrival, August 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I would prefer it if my learned friend would just ask the witness to describe how it functioned or something of that nature, because it does imply a chain of command which didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the functioning of the armed forces is a total different question as a chain of command, as such. A chain of command is another observation than how it functioned because that gave way to a certain opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's what appeared in the question, chain of command. That's what I was objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Appearing in the question doesn't mean it was how it functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first question ought to have been whether there was a chain of command that he is aware of as far as the Territorial Defence in Srebrenica is concerned. So answer that question first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't aware of the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it. Yes, Mr. Wubben, I don't think we need to proceed any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Was there any command within the Territorial Defence in Srebrenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: There was an organ, I'd rather say, called the staff of Territorial Defence, made up by the commanders of the units that were present in the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And my next question is: This staff of the TO, was that staff also headed by a supreme commander, if so?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: The supreme commander of the armed forces is the War Presidency, and Naser Oric was commander of the defence of Srebrenica, as it was called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we are entering into a confusion zone, as I see it. You, in answering a question that was put to you earlier on, you said that when you transferred to the Srebrenica hospital there, you essentially became part of the armed forces of Srebrenica. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, not only upon my arrival in Srebrenica. I became a member of the Territorial Defence in May 1992, a Territorial Defence which was later to become the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when I arrived to the war hospital in Kalesija. Since then, and until I was demobilised, I was a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was, therefore, in this capacity that I spent my time in Srebrenica as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you said that you had also been appointed as chief medical officer of the Srebrenica, et cetera, in September, August -- August or September of 1992; do you remember that? And that as such, you formed part of the military set-up there. Yes. Who were -- who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the operations staff since the second half of September 1992, that is, of the operations staff of the Territorial Defence of Srebrenica. And at the time it was already called the armed forces of Srebrenica. According to this structure, Osman Osmanovic, chief of staff, was my superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And who was Osman Osmanovic's superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Osman Osmanovic was chief of staff, and his superior at the time was Commander Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I please clarify also with respect to my questions were focusing, indeed, on August and perhaps beginning of September, because then there is this change in staff. And I will refer to that also with a few --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead for the time. I apologise to you for having interrupted you, but we need to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the Territorial Defence, was there at the time in August already a staff functioning?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a Territorial Defence staff, and I've already stayed that it was made up mostly of the commanders of the local units present in the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And who headed that staff of local commanders? Who was chairing that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, if anyone. It may be that it's completely disorganised and that needs to be left open rather than it being suggested to the witness that there was necessarily a commander, which there might not have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I think that's a perfectly legitimate objection. It's a question of how you phrase your questions, that's all, Mr. Wubben, because ultimately we will get there just the same, I mean we will get to that question. When you refer -- no, I will not phrase the question for you. It's your problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you took part of such a staff or a staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not take any part in the work of the Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Was Naser Oric, to your knowledge, part of that staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can you give me the names of local commanders and their units who formed part of that staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to remember them. The units were established on the territorial principle, according to the area they were established in, so that the Territorial Defence unit in Suceska was commanded by Zulfo Tursunovic. The units active in the south-east of the Srebrenica municipality, namely Kragljevode, Osmace, Skenderovici, were, I believe, commanded by Nedzad Bektic, Senaid Tabakovic, and I don't recall who else there was. And the unit of the Territorial Defence in Biljega was commanded by Ahmo Tihic. As for the town proper of Srebrenica, there were two units, one commanded by Atif Ustic and the other by Hakija Meholjic. There were also units in the south-east of the Srebrenica enclave, namely, the areas of Potocari, Pale, Likari, but I don't recall who the commanders of these units were. So when I said that the staff comprised commanders of these units, I meant to say that it was a rather informal group of people who simply conferred to see how they could effectively stand ground and put up resistance and defend Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I have a question with regard to a staff meeting. You referred to this staff meeting as a couple of local commanders, but is it correct that you, for yourself, met with Naser Oric and some of his men at the PTT building for a staff meeting, in August?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: The PTT building was opposite the hospital, some 30 metres from -- across the hospital. Oftentimes, time and work permitting, I would cross the street and meet different people there, talking to them informally. So I never took part in any formal meeting of a staff or any other military institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And what about an informal meeting, a discussion together with staff? Were you ever present at such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall taking part in any meetings in this particular period, in this one month. It was rather that I was getting to know these people, because you have to know that it was my first time in Srebrenica at the time. I knew no one. I didn't even know where Srebrenica was located earlier on. And this is why I used my spare time to get to know the people there, and we talked about different matters, among other things, how to defend ourselves from the attack and the aggression best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Mujkanovic, I will proceed to show you a number of documents, and as much as possible - original documents - ask you for -- most of them, for your comments. In relation to that, I have a prior question. Will you please clarify or confirm whether or not you are familiar with the signature of Naser Oric at the times in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have to start with that question first and foremost, Mr. Wubben, and ask the witness to explain to us how come, if he is familiar with Naser Oric's signature, how come he is familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I thought, Your Honour, with all respect, that that was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't understand it to be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the signature of Naser Oric at the time in -- at your time in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, I had occasion to -- when I would receive a slip of paper from Naser Oric at times when he was unable to reach the hospital but was interested in knowing what the condition of certain patients was, or when he had some private matter he would inquire me about, to see his signature on such slips of paper and to become familiarised with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did that happen often, throughout the period of time during the hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Not that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: What was the meaning of those papers signed by him? Was there a special function?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Were -- these papers signed by Naser Oric, were these special documents or other kinds of documents, papers?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: These were no documents. These were simply messages on slips of paper. And it was in March or April 1993 that this practice intensified, when refugees were already fleeing from Srebrenica to Tuzla, that he would want to get in touch with me personally and could not otherwise because he was occupied, because this was at the time of the most intensive attacks on Srebrenica. It was from early April until the 17th of April, 1993, when he would send messages to me to the effect that certain wounded people had to be evacuated before some others, and matters to that effect. So these were no documents, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I need now the assistance of the usher. Please, will you put on the ELMO Exhibit number 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say that we -- based on what this witness has said, we would object to this witness being asked to authenticate the signature of Naser Oric. In our submission, there hasn't isn't a sufficient foundation. In most legal systems, I imagine around the world, there are two or three ways of proofing -- of proving signature, either by the person who wrote it or the person who saw the person actual sign the document, or by someone who has corresponded regularly with the person. I have extracts from the relevant law in the United Kingdom. I gather it's the same in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it's not a question of weight, it's a question of admissibility. If a person is just going to, in our submission, guess that something is a signature from 12 years ago, we would submit that that's unsafe, that's a very unsafe procedure to be permitted. In our submission, that there is insufficient foundation for this witness to purport to authenticate the signatures of Naser Oric. And if it's a matter we need to go into, I have extracts from Archibald just to show what the procedure is in the United Kingdom. I imagine it's the same in Your Honours' jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I don't think you're exempted from answering that. Certainly guessing is one thing. But looking at a signature and telling us if, according to him, that signature resembles the one he knows to be of Naser Oric, that's definitely admissible, and that's how we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's already told us that -- of course we are not proving that that is, indeed, the signature of Naser Oric because the witness is telling us so. But the witness, of course, has every right to be asked a question by the Prosecution whether, to him, that is the signature of Naser Oric. Then we decide whether it's the signature of Naser Oric or not later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that point, Your Honour. My objection is to say is there's insufficient foundation because he neither saw the document signed by Oric and he hasn't corresponded regularly with him. And so our submission is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's exactly that. He told us that he used to receive regularly these notes from -- according to him, from Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My objection is on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What I wanted to know is whether these notes were signed by -- were signed in any way. Were they signed? And how were they signed? These notes that Mr. Wubben asked you about, that you told us that used to receive inquiring about patients in the hospital, you said they would be from Naser Oric. How would you know that they would be from Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would be brought over by a courier who told me, "These were sent to you by Naser Oric." These would even by incomplete slips of paper containing a message, saying Please do this or that, or Could you please help with this or that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were they usually signed, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were always signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how were they signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were signed in hand, at the end of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but what would the signature say? Would it say "Naser Oric"? Would it say "Oric"? Would it say "Naser"? What would it say, or what would it show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a signature. Not a name and a surname but a signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just very, in brief, my response to Defence counsel would be: That criterion is not as stated by him but a ruling by your own Chamber in October, that when it comes to authentication everything is admitted unless your Chamber finds out it is manifestly inappropriate. And that is a wider range --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time, Mr. Wubben. Let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: On Sanction there is, Your Honour, the English translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I want to see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: -- on the ELMO is the document. Can the usher please show the document on the ELMO, if so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can we be told which document it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Document 73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P73? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: P73, yes. And P73 is -- has the ERN number 02075808.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My question is: Do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: This signature does look like Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I refer now to the text, Dr. Mujkanovic. The text is headed, and I'll read out: "Srebrenica TO," and the date with the place, Bajramovici, 20th of May, 1992, a decision. And the wording goes: "The Srebrenica municipal TO staff is hereby informed ..." Now, the list goes on "as the following shall be appointed to the Srebrenica TO staff." And I quote: "Naser Oric, as commander of the Srebrenica TO staff ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness can read.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please read the names, Dr. Mujkanovic, as suggested by the Judge, from 1 up to 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Give him a chance to read it, and then put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujkanovic, these names and the positions mentioned, are these names and positions consistent with your experience from August 1992 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I know some of the people named here; others I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: And who do you know of the list? Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I know Naser Oric, Atif Ustic, Zulfo Tursunovic, Hamdija. I know Bogilovic Becir, but I don't Sevket Djozic and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the last name. You said you didn't know Sevket Djozic and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ahmo Tihic. But I didn't know Djozic Sevket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you know Ahmo Tihic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was only one person you didn't know from this list, and that was Sevket Djozic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My next question is: Now, those names you know, at the time in Srebrenica, from August, were the positions linked to those names consistent with your experience in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew some of them, and some I didn't. I knew about Atif Ustic, that he was commander of Suceska, or rather, commander of the unit in Srebrenica. I knew about Zulfo Tursunovic, that he was commander of Suceska. Hamdija Fejzic, I didn't know that he was in commander of anything. Sevket, I didn't know. Bogilovic, I didn't know, and I knew that Ahmo Tihic, that he was in the area of Biljega, that he was commander there. But I learned about this later on, not the moment I arrived in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But did you experience that these persons are functioning in that position, as mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Did you know of their position, as such, as you confirm it now, today, for the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't understand that. He just said that he didn't have experience of it. If he's then being asked, Well, do you know if they occupied those positions, then fine. But what's he supposed to have confirmed today before the Judges? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Jones. Would you rephrase the question if you, indeed, want to put that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Was it known to you, at the time you were in Srebrenica, that -- and I'll start with the names you're familiar with, that Naser Oric was commander of the TO staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben, I hate to interrupt you, but he's already told us each, one by one. I think barely a minute ago he went through the whole list and said what he knew as far as the position occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: So far, Your Honour, he has not confirmed that with respect to Naser Oric, so I will repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. All right. Ask him about Naser Oric only, because the rest he has -- although even I think I heard him say so, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I might be mistaken, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. Go ahead, but ask that question only, please, and let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Can you confirm that it was known to your experience that Naser Oric was, indeed, commander of the Srebrenica TO staff at the days of your stay in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Srebrenica from the 5th of August to the 22nd of April. You must specify the period of time you have in mind. During the nine months I stayed there, I knew that he was commander, and I knew who was which commander. But are we talking about early September 1992? Because that's how you read you. If we're talking about that period in time, I knew nothing about how the Territorial Defence was structured, nor did I want to know. Occasionally, I met some of the local commanders, but I was not aware of a formal body named "Staff," nor did I know that the staff was led by Naser Oric. I knew that Naser Oric was commander of the Srebrenica defence, but I was unaware of how this functioned in terms of structure and organisation, or any possible links. I didn't want to know. I can talk about the second half of September, when I formally became a member of the operations staff. Now, this is something that perhaps I could tell you about, but I'm afraid I can't tell you anything prior to my arrival, or about the first month following my arrival. I had no real desire to know more about the structure or organisation of the military bodies. I knew nothing about how these were structured. I must say that, even if a specific structure was in place, it certainly didn't work in the way that some of these documents seemed to suggest. The only thing that happened was people were trying to get themselves organised to fend off the attacks of the army of Republika Srpska and the army of Yugoslavia. Most of the villages had their own units. They had guards. People were holding the line to keep the enemy from breaking through, storming the villages and massacring the local population. Now, whether two or three or four months after the aggression broke out someone actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I apologise, Dr. Mujkanovic, you answered my question. Thank you for that, and let's limit the answering of my questions towards the issues, and I apologise for interrupting you. Let's go to the following document, P74.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Usher, please, will you assist me. P74, ERN 02075809.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Witness, will you please take a look at this document and the signature. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: It is quite illegible. Half of the signature is covered by a stamp. Based on what I see here, I'm unable to confirm whether this looks anything like Mr. Oric's signature. The other half of the signature may, perhaps, be a little like it, but I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: My question relates -- my following question relates to the content of this document. It is a decision dated -- Bajramovici, 20 May 1992 and I quote: "Becir Bogilovic" - further on - "appointed the temporary police commander in the town of Srebrenica." Within the statement of reasons, and I quote: "Becir Bogilovic is hereby tasked with gathering policemen and reviving of the service for protecting law and order." Did you read that, Dr. Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Is, according to your experience, this decision being implemented in practice in your time at Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which time? You need to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: August and later on.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I met Becir Bogilovic perhaps a month after I arrived in Srebrenica. The position he held then was chief of the public security station. I have no idea about the date of his appointment, or pursuant to which specific decision he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: But was he acting as being in charge of the temporary police or the police in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about temporary. There was civilian police. Whether it was of a permanent or temporary nature is not something that I can say. But there was a civilian police presence in the town of Srebrenica. And as I said, when I met Becir Bogilovic, he was chief of the public security station in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Next document, usher, please, P75, ERN number 02075808 -- again, please, 020705810.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Please take a look at the document, Dr. Mujkanovic. My question is: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: It looks like Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In this document -- in this document, persons are mentioned. Will you please read the redaction under "Decision." That's the persons at 1, 2, 3.

utterances.speaker: NEDRET MUJKANOVIC
utterances.text: I've read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Now, this is a decision of the 26th of May, 1992, of the Territorial Defence staff, a decision to expand the Srebrenica TO staff with new members. Those names, is it, to your -- is it -- is that consistent with your experience that those people named in that decision did take part of the Srebrenica TO staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, a couple of points, really. First is we've objected to the authenticity of all these documents, but if it's anything it's a purported decision, we're not accepting, and it shouldn't be suggested that this is a decision that we all know is a decision of the TO Staff that may be a forgery. But secondly, I'm sure we've all noted that the date is May. We're talking about three months before this witness arrived, and he's also said repeatedly that he doesn't know the structure of the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, he didn't know the structure in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. But it's just the -- the inherent suggestiveness of showing him document after document of possibly false or forged documents and saying, Is this -- Is your experience consistent with the facts stated here, is, in my submission, is going to lead to very misleading evidence being given. It would be a lot simpler if Mr. Wubben would just say: Atif Krdzic to say, Do you know him, do you know what his function was in August? In fact, an exercise -- we could even dispense with the documents. He could simply ask -- ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll slow down. He could simply ask questions about people and their functions, and if later he wants to match that up with the documents, then fine. But to place document after document in front of this witness and try to get him to confirm that somehow these documents have any value is, in my submission, objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go about it in a different manner. Witness, you have read that this document that you have been handed by our usher, there are three names there, Atif Krdzic, Nedzad Bektic, Senaid Tabakovic. Did you know these persons, or did you come to know these persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I met Atif Krdzic sometime in September of 1992. I met Nedzad Bektic in late September 1992. I met Senaid Tabakovic sometime in November 1992. I did meet these people. I told you when I met them. But again, I can't confirm the authenticity of this decision simply because it was written, produced, at a time when I was still not in the Srebrenica area.
